newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ investment experts rate pension scheme highly.
newsitem.headline: NZ investment experts rate pension scheme highly.

text.p: New Zealand investment experts awarded a "pretty high pass rate" to a compulsory retirement savings scheme unveiled on Monday by Treasurer Winston Peters.
Opponents predict a resounding defeat when the scheme, widely seen as an opinion poll on Peters, is put to a public referendum in September.
But investment experts, while loath to suggest which way people should vote, gave Peters a vote of confidence by saying they were now reassured the scheme to be voted on was sound.

"Our reaction is strongly positive. We feel they've done a very good job in the design of a workable and practical scheme. It's now over to the voters to actually assess it," Roger Gill, chief executive of the Investment Savings and Insurance Association (ISI), told Reuters.
Gill said the design team had done well in coming to grips with a complex issue, and the scheme included to varying degrees all the features the ISI saw as essential.
"Overall it receives a pretty high pass rate," he said.
AMP Investments general manager Rodney Cook agreed.
"I'm not seeking to advocate one form of scheme over another, but if the country is philosophically ready for a compulsory superannuation scheme, then this seems to be a pretty good one," he said.
A government white paper published earlier on Monday said the pension scheme would require all earners who can to save about NZ$120,000 ($81,000) toward the cost of their pension.

The scheme would initially require workers to contribute three percent of their income to the scheme. On retirement, the savings would be used to buy an annuity to deliver income equivalent to the current state pension.
The contribution level would rise to eight percent of income over five years, provided the government can afford the tax cuts it has promised in order to offset the higher contributions.
Compensatory tax cuts are guaranteed in the first year, but thereafter would only happen "when fiscally sustainable".
AMP's Cook welcomed news that tax cuts and contribution increases were inextricably linked.

"Contribution levels won't be rising...until broadly similar tax cuts can be passed on. The really important message for the community and the government there is that the government has to stay responsible and run budget surpluses, otherwise how are we
going to be given tax cuts in the future?"
Cook said AMP's concerns about the affordability of government top-ups to individual savings had been addressed by the scheme's 40-year phase-in period.

He said the suggested contribution collection methods seemed sensible, and the scheme's designers had taken seriously the concerns raised by women who said their lower earnings, shorter average working life and longer life expectancy could disadvantage them.
Peters outlined a planned equalisation payment for women so their annuity had the same value as men's without costing more in contributions.
"The only practical issue that is yet to be resolved is the deduction of superannuation contributions from your investment income at source," Cook said.
The compulsory pension scheme, to be implemented in July next year if passed in the referendum, was a key part of the election campaign of Peters' party, New Zealand First.
NZ First is the junior partner in a coalition with the conservative National Party.
A recent poll of 933 people by financial services group Colonial showed opposition to the scheme had risen to 63 percent from 59 percent in May.
